questions.question: Define the five forces that act on materials, give an everyday example of each, and explain how bending and torsion are built from the simpler forces.
questions.expected_answer: Tension pulls a material so it stretches (washing-line wire); compression pushes so it shortens (brick at the base of a wall); bending acts across a supported member so one side stretches and the other squashes (shelf sagging under books); torsion twists one end relative to the other (screwdriver shaft, wringing a towel); shear is a pair of opposite forces sliding one part past another (scissors, a bolt between pulled plates). Bending is tension on the outer curve and compression on the inner curve with an unstretched neutral axis between them; torsion is shear acting all around the outside of a shaft as each layer slides past its neighbour.

questions.question: Distinguish strength, stiffness, elasticity, brittleness and toughness, and compare how concrete, steel and timber respond to tension and compression.
questions.expected_answer: Strength is the greatest stress a material carries before breaking and must be named with the force (tensile, compressive, shear). Stiffness is resistance to deformation while loaded. Elasticity is returning to shape when the load is removed, up to the elastic limit, beyond which deformation is permanent. Brittleness is breaking with little deformation or warning; toughness is absorbing much energy and deforming greatly before breaking. Concrete is strong in compression, about one tenth as strong in tension, and brittle. Steel is strong and tough in both tension and compression. Timber is strong along the grain, weak across it and splits along the grain in shear.

questions.question: Describe a fair classroom test for one of the five forces, state the rules of fair testing, and explain why a straw that buckles should not be recorded as weak in compression.
questions.expected_answer: Example: bending test with a ruler, card strip and corrugated card strip of equal length and width, each rested between two bricks and loaded at the midpoint with coins added one at a time until failure; record material, dimensions, breaking load and how it failed. Fair testing: change one variable at a time, use specimens of equal size, load at the same point and rate, repeat tests, and record results in a table. A slender straw bows sideways and collapses before its material reaches crushing strength; that is buckling, which depends on length and slenderness rather than material strength, so it is recorded as buckled and fixed by a shorter or braced member, not a stronger material.
